extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms for issuing, honoring, and responding to news/press embargoes — the practice of asking media not to publish information until a specified date or condition. Covers typical uses (product, medical, government announcements), ethical considerations, enforcement and consequences of breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a news/press embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: A news embargo or press embargo is a request or requirement by a source that the information or news provided by that source not be published until a certain date or certain conditions have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargoes are often used by businesses making product announcements, by medical journals, and by government officials announcing policy initiatives; the media is given advance knowledge so reports can be prepared to coincide with the announcement date and still meet press time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embargoes to enable prepared, timely coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes give journalists advance knowledge of details being held secret so that reports can be prepared to coincide with the announcement date and yet still meet press time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because journalists have time to prepare, embargoes theoretically reduce inaccuracy in reporting by reducing incentives to rush stories to 'scoop' competitors; they enable production of backgrounders that accompany initial coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review embargoes for early-access reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Review embargoes: reviewers are given early access to content or products in exchange for keeping review results secret until the embargo is lifted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in video games, computer hardware and films to prevent inaccurate early reviews, avoid harming launch sales, and to allow time to fix flaws/bugs discovered by reviewers before public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes typically function as a 'gentlemen's agreement'
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes are usually arranged in advance as 'gentlemen's agreements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes publicists send embargoed press releases unsolicited hoping newsrooms will respect the date without having first agreed; such informal nature affects enforceability and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling releases: 'For Immediate Release' signals no embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'For Immediate Release' often found at the top of press releases indicates that the information in the release is not embargoed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers of releases should label embargoed material clearly (and conversely avoid 'For Immediate Release' if they expect the item to remain embargoed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for breaking an embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: If the embargo is broken by reporting before then, the source will retaliate by restricting access to further information by that journalist or their publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking an embargo is typically considered a serious breach of trust and can result in the offending outlet being barred from receiving advance information for a long period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental versus intentional embargo breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations sometimes break embargoes and report information before the embargo expires, either accidentally (due to miscommunication in the newsroom) or intentionally (to get the jump on their competitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional breaches may be defended as 'scoops' (example: Piers Morgan breaking a BBC embargo), but still draw criticism and reputational consequences; accidental breaches point to internal process failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes as a tool that can influence media presentation (ethical concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: News embargoes are one of several ways a source can influence media presentation of the information they provide; others include providing information 'on background' or 'not for attribution', limiting or providing 'access', or direct intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' reactions to these influence tactics are a matter of journalistic ethics; critics argue embargoes (especially in medical publishing) can be driven by profit motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockup procedures for sensitive government announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to release of budgets and other important government announcements, reporters are held in a 'lockup' so they can prepare stories in advance and are not permitted to file until after the official announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lockups are aimed at preventing insider trading and synchronizing coverage; examples include budget lockups in Canada, Australia and IMF/central-bank-style embargoes timed for global markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/journal embargo practices (Ingelfinger rule / JAMA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical journals commonly apply embargoes to health-related news regarding upcoming articles; major journals have publication embargoes with specified timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: JAMA's embargo holds until 15:00 Central Time on the day before the cover date; journalists receive advance copies and selected articles have press releases/news videos prepared. Reasons given: enable more accurate coverage and allow doctors/scientists to analyze studies before the public; criticisms include potential profit motives of journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes used to coordinate market/public effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Some embargoes are timed to synchronise effect across markets or jurisdictions (e.g., IMF biweekly briefings embargoed until a specific time to synchronise global stock-market effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coordinating global release, specify precise embargo lift times in multiple time zones and communicate clearly to participating outlets to avoid premature publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo may be rescinded or end if leaked or circumstances change
rubrics_metrics.description: If embargoed information leaks or circumstances change (e.g., security concerns), the source may agree to end the embargo or remove the person/item from risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ministry of Defence embargo on Prince Harry serving in Afghanistan ended after leaks and officials agreed to end the embargo; producers should plan for contingency actions if leaks occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes can be instigated by non-source actors (self-censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: An embargo-like suppression can be instigated by media organizations or others rather than the original source (self-censorship), as when outlets agreed to suppress reporting (e.g., The New York Times and the kidnapping of David Rohde).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that not all 'embargoes' are source-imposed; journalistic decisions to withhold can arise from safety, legal or ethical concerns and carry different obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations and journalistic expectations when issuing embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuers should understand that embargoes depend on mutual trust and clear communication; journalists should weigh the ethical implications of accepting and honoring embargoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: clearly state embargo terms (exact date/time/conditions), communicate with intended outlets, and avoid sending unsolicited embargoed material without prior agreement; journalists should verify embargo terms and have internal processes to avoid accidental breaches.
